# Database Storage and Transaction Internals: Technical Brief

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES** (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) is the canonical WAL-based recovery protocol. Every page modification generates a log record tagged with a monotonically increasing **LSN (log sequence number)**, stored both in the log and stamped on the data page itself (`PageLSN`). The WAL invariant requires that a page's `PageLSN`-covering log record reach stable storage before the page itself is flushed, and that no transaction's commit be acknowledged until its log records are durable (**log force-at-commit**). To avoid forcing a log flush per transaction, systems use **group commit**: multiple concurrent commit requests batch into a single `fsync`, amortizing the durability cost. ARIES uses **physiological logging** — physical at the page level but logical within the page (e.g., "insert record R at logical slot position") — which is more compact than full physical before/after images and tolerant of a page's internal layout changing between log and redo time.

**Checkpointing** limits how far back recovery must scan. ARIES uses **fuzzy checkpoints**: a checkpoint record captures the current transaction table and dirty page table without forcing all dirty pages to disk, avoiding a stop-the-world flush; recovery then uses the checkpoint's recorded dirty-page LSNs to determine the correct redo start point. This differs from a **consistent checkpoint**, which blocks new updates and flushes all dirty pages before finishing, guaranteeing no replay is needed but at a severe availability cost. **Compensation Log Records (CLRs)** are written during transaction rollback/undo; they record the logical inverse of an undone operation and carry a pointer (`UndoNxtLSN`) to the next record to undo, making undo **idempotent** — if a crash interrupts rollback, redo of CLRs will not re-undo already-undone work, since CLRs themselves are never undone.

Real systems diverge in implementation: **PostgreSQL's WAL** logs physical full-page images periodically (to guard against torn pages) and otherwise logical/physiological deltas, with `wal_level` controlling whether replication-sufficient detail is logged. **InnoDB's redo log** is a circular physical log of page-level changes combined with a **doublewrite buffer** for torn-page protection (below). **SQLite** instead offers a choice between a **rollback journal** (pre-image before-write, truncated at commit) and **WAL mode**, where committed pages are appended to a separate WAL file and periodically checkpointed into the main database file — closer in spirit to log-structured buffering than ARIES-style redo/undo logging.

## 2. MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

**Snapshot isolation (SI)** is the dominant MVCC isolation level. Each transaction is assigned a start timestamp (or snapshot) and sees only versions committed before that point; writes create new versions rather than overwriting in place. PostgreSQL implements this via **tuple-level `xmin`/`xmax` fields**: `xmin` is the transaction ID that created a row version, `xmax` is the transaction ID that deleted/superseded it (or invalid if the version is still live). Visibility is determined by consulting a **snapshot** (a set of transaction IDs considered in-progress at snapshot-acquisition time) and the commit status recorded in `pg_xact` (formerly `pg_clog`). This is an **append-only MVCC** design: old versions remain in the heap as dead tuples until **VACUUM** reclaims them, which can only happen once no active transaction's snapshot could still need them — determined by the **oldest active transaction's xmin**, sometimes called the xmin horizon.

The alternative is **undo-log-based MVCC**, used by Oracle and InnoDB: updates happen in place, and the previous version is pushed into a rollback segment (Oracle) or undo log (InnoDB), chained via pointers so that a reader needing an old snapshot reconstructs it by walking undo records backward. This avoids heap bloat but adds undo-log maintenance and purge overhead instead of vacuum overhead.

Pure snapshot isolation does not guarantee serializability: it admits **write skew**, where two transactions each read overlapping data, make disjoint writes based on that read, and both commit, violating an invariant that spans both writes (the classic example: two on-call doctors each check that at least one other doctor is on call before taking themselves off call). **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, implemented in PostgreSQL, detects this by tracking **rw-antidependencies** (one transaction reads a value another concurrently writes) and aborting a transaction when a **"dangerous structure"** — two consecutive rw-antidependency edges forming a cycle risk — is detected among concurrent transactions, rather than requiring full conflict serializability checking.

Conflict resolution on concurrent writes to the same version follows either **first-committer-wins** (the transaction that commits first succeeds; the later one gets a serialization failure, used by Postgres) or **first-updater-wins** (the first transaction to attempt the write acquires a lock and blocks others, used by some other SI implementations). Underlying both is **timestamp ordering (T/O)**: each version carries a write timestamp, and the **Thomas Write Rule** allows a stale write to be silently ignored (rather than aborted) if no transaction has read the version the ignored write would have overwritten and a later write has already superseded it — an optimization over strict multi-version timestamp ordering (MVTO), which otherwise aborts any write older than the latest read timestamp on the item. **Optimistic concurrency control (OCC)** instead defers conflict detection to a validation phase at commit, checking whether the transaction's read set was modified by any transaction that committed during its execution, aborting on conflict rather than blocking during execution.

## 3. LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge Trees)

Writes land first in a **memtable**, an in-memory sorted structure (commonly a **skiplist**, as in RocksDB and Cassandra) that supports efficient ordered insertion and range scan. For durability before the memtable is flushed, writes are also appended to a **WAL** specific to the memtable's generation; on crash, the WAL is replayed to reconstruct the memtable's contents. When a memtable reaches a size threshold, it is flushed as an immutable, sorted **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** to disk — a file format with data blocks plus a sparse **block index** keyed by the first key of each block, allowing binary search to a block before a linear scan within it.

Because SSTables are immutable and multiple generations accumulate, **compaction** merges them to bound the number of files a read must check and to reclaim space from overwritten/deleted keys. **Size-tiered compaction** groups SSTables of similar size and merges them into a larger one when enough accumulate at a tier (used historically in Cassandra); it has lower write amplification but higher space amplification and read amplification, since a key may exist in many same-tier files. **Leveled compaction (LCS)**, used in RocksDB's default and LevelDB, organizes SSTables into levels `L0..Ln` of exponentially increasing size; within a level (except L0) key ranges are non-overlapping, so compaction merges one SSTable from level `Li` with the overlapping SSTables in `Li+1`, bounding the number of files a point lookup must check per level at the cost of higher write amplification (each key gets rewritten roughly once per level it passes through). RocksDB also supports **universal compaction**, a tiered scheme favoring write throughput over read/space amplification, and hybrid tiered+leveled schemes that apply size-tiering to upper levels and leveling lower in the hierarchy.

**Bloom filters** attached to each SSTable allow point lookups to skip SSTables that provably do not contain a key, trading a tunable false-positive rate (configured via bits-per-key) for avoiding disk I/O on keys absent from a given SSTable; they cannot be used to skip range scans since they don't preserve order information. **Deletes** are represented as **tombstones** — markers recording that a key was deleted at a given sequence number — which must propagate through compactions and are only physically dropped once compacted past the oldest snapshot/read that might still need to observe the deletion, otherwise a delete could be "undone" by exposing an older, pre-delete version still present in a lower level. The overall LSM design trades increased **write amplification** (each key is rewritten across multiple compaction passes) and some **read amplification** (a lookup may check memtable, L0, and potentially several levels) for drastically improved write throughput relative to in-place B+tree updates, since writes are always sequential appends rather than random-access page writes.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

Insertions that overflow a leaf trigger a **node split**: the leaf's keys are divided roughly in half, a new sibling leaf is allocated, and the median key is propagated up to the parent as a new separator, potentially cascading splits up to the root (**root split**, which increases tree height by one). Deletions that underflow a node trigger **merging** with a sibling, or **redistribution** (borrowing a key from a sibling) if the sibling has slack capacity, keeping node occupancy above a configured **fill-factor** threshold (commonly 50%) to bound tree height and avoid pathological sparsity. Many production systems (e.g., InnoDB) use **bulk loading** with sequential **right-only appends** when initially populating an index from sorted input, avoiding repeated splits by filling each leaf near capacity directly.

Structure Modification Operations (**SMOs**) — splits, merges, and root changes — are the central concurrency-control challenge in B+tree implementations, since naively locking the whole path during an SMO serializes all concurrent traversals. **Latch crabbing** (also called lock coupling) is the classic traversal protocol: a reader/writer acquires a latch on a child node before releasing the latch on its parent, holding at most two node latches at a time; for inserts/deletes, a traversal optimistically takes read latches down the tree and only escalates to write latches on nodes if it determines a split/merge might propagate to them (determined by checking whether a node is "safe," i.e. has slack capacity so no SMO is needed).

**B-link trees (B-link trees / "blink trees")** relax strict latch crabbing further: every node gets a **right-sibling pointer**, and a split initially only links the new sibling in via that pointer without immediately updating the parent's separator key, allowing the split to be committed as two independent atomic steps rather than one multi-node critical section. A concurrent reader that lands on a node mid-split simply follows the right-sibling pointer if its target key isn't present, rather than blocking. This also gives blink trees a recovery benefit: if a crash occurs between the child-level split and the parent-level separator insertion, the right-sibling pointer alone is sufficient to keep the tree navigable and correct, so recovery can lazily repair the missing parent entry rather than treating it as a corruption. **Foster trees** extend this idea further by introducing a temporary "foster child" pointer that lets a struct­ural change be deferred and executed as an independent, restartable sub-operation, reducing the scope of latching needed per SMO even further than blink trees.

Index size and I/O efficiency are improved via **prefix/suffix key truncation**: internal separator keys need only be long enough to discriminate between two subtrees, so a full leaf key is often truncated to its minimal distinguishing prefix when promoted as an internal separator, and leaf keys sharing a common prefix with their neighbors can be prefix-compressed within a page.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

2PC is an **atomic commitment protocol**, not a consensus protocol — it guarantees all participants reach the same (commit or abort) decision but does not by itself tolerate coordinator failure the way a consensus protocol like Paxos does; this distinction matters because 2PC alone can **block** indefinitely. In the **prepare (voting) phase**, the coordinator sends a `PREPARE` message to all participants; each participant durably writes a prepare log record (via WAL) recording its intent and locks the needed resources, then replies `VOTE-COMMIT` or `VOTE-ABORT`. If all votes are commit, the coordinator durably logs the decision and enters the **commit phase**, broadcasting `COMMIT`; any single `VOTE-ABORT` instead triggers a broadcast `ABORT`. Participants ack, and the coordinator can then forget the transaction.

The core failure mode is the **blocking problem**: if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted commit but before the decision is broadcast, those participants are **in-doubt** — holding locks, unable to unilaterally decide commit or abort, since another participant might have voted abort or the coordinator might decide either way upon recovery. They must block until the coordinator recovers and replays its log, or until a separate recovery/coordinator-election protocol resolves it. **Three-phase commit (3PC)** addresses this by inserting a **PreCommit** phase between voting and committing: phases become **CanCommit → PreCommit → DoCommit**. Because PreCommit is only sent once the coordinator knows all votes were commit, and participants can time out and safely elect a new coordinator using the PreCommit state (since that state guarantees all participants are already known to have voted commit), 3PC avoids blocking under a bounded, synchronous failure model — but it isn't used widely in practice because it assumes bounded message delays and doesn't tolerate network partitions cleanly.

Two logging optimizations reduce 2PC's cost. **Presumed abort** lets the coordinator skip writing or retaining log records for aborted transactions: if a participant queries about a transaction the coordinator has no record of, it presumes abort, since the coordinator only needs to persist records for transactions it decided to commit. **Presumed commit** inverts this for workloads dominated by commits, logging only abort decisions and presuming commit for unknown transactions, at the cost of needing an extra round in the protocol to collect acknowledgments before the coordinator can safely forget a commit decision.

Industrially, the **XA standard** (X/Open Distributed Transaction Processing) defines the interface between a transaction manager (coordinator) and resource managers (participants, e.g., databases or message queues), implemented via **JTA (Java Transaction API)** in Java environments, letting heterogeneous resource managers participate in a single 2PC-coordinated transaction. **Google Spanner** layers 2PC on top of **Paxos**: each shard (Paxos group) uses Paxos for intra-shard replication and leader election, while cross-shard transactions use 2PC among the Paxos group leaders, with **TrueTime**-derived commit timestamps providing external consistency — Paxos handles replica-failure consensus, while 2PC handles cross-shard atomicity, illustrating that the two protocols solve different problems and are often composed rather than substituted for one another.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport clocks** assign each process a monotonically increasing integer counter. On any local event, the process increments its own counter; on sending a message, it attaches the current counter value; on receiving a message with timestamp `t`, the process sets its counter to `max(local, t) + 1`. This produces a **partial order consistent with happens-before**: if event A happens-before event B (causally), then `LC(A) < LC(B)`, but the converse doesn't hold — two causally unrelated (concurrent) events can still receive comparable timestamps. A **total order** for cases that need one (e.g., deterministic tie-breaking) is obtained by extending the comparison with process IDs as a tiebreaker, but this total order is arbitrary with respect to causality for concurrent events, not a reflection of real concurrency.

**Vector clocks** fix the inability to detect concurrency. Each process `i` keeps a vector `V` of length `n` (one entry per process); on a local event, process `i` increments `V[i]`; on sending, it attaches `V`; on receiving a message with vector `W`, the receiving process computes `V[k] = max(V[k], W[k])` for every index `k`, then increments its own entry. Two events are causally ordered if one vector **dominates** the other elementwise; they're **concurrent** if neither vector dominates (incomparable vectors) — this is the critical extra power over Lamport clocks: vector clocks can detect true concurrency, not just produce a consistent order. The cost is `O(n)` space and message overhead per timestamp, which becomes problematic as cluster size grows, motivating pruning/garbage-collection heuristics in practice.

**Version vectors** are a related but distinct mechanism: rather than timestamping *events* across all processes, they track, per data item, a vector of (replica, counter) pairs representing which replica versions contributed to the item's current value. Systems like **Amazon Dynamo**, Riak, and Voldemort attach version vectors to objects so that on a read encountering divergent versions from different replicas, the client or system can determine whether one version vector dominates another (meaning one write strictly supersedes the other) or whether they're concurrent, in which case the conflicting versions are surfaced to the application (or merged via a CRDT-style policy) rather than one being silently discarded.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)**, used in CockroachDB and MongoDB, combine a physical-time component with a logical counter: the clock value is normally just the node's physical clock, but when causal dependencies would otherwise violate monotonicity (e.g., receiving a message timestamped ahead of the local physical clock), the logical counter increments to preserve the happens-before guarantee while keeping the timestamp bounded close to physical time (bounded divergence), unlike pure Lamport clocks whose relation to wall-clock time is unconstrained. This matters for databases because HLC timestamps can double as both causal-ordering tokens and approximately-real-time snapshot/commit timestamps usable for time-bounded staleness reads.

**Spanner's TrueTime** takes a different approach entirely: rather than a logical clock, it exposes physical time with an explicit, bounded uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` (bounded by `epsilon`), derived from GPS and atomic clock references. Spanner's **commit-wait** rule has a transaction coordinator delay making a commit visible until the TrueTime interval guarantees the commit timestamp is in the past for all observers, which yields **external consistency** (if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts in real time, T1's timestamp is less than T2's) without needing message-passing-based logical clocks at all — the uncertainty bound substitutes for causal tracking.

## 7. Quorum Systems

The **Dynamo-style N/R/W model** parameterizes replication by a replication factor `N` (number of replicas per key), a read quorum `R`, and a write quorum `W`: a write succeeds once `W` replicas acknowledge it, a read succeeds once `R` replicas respond and their versions are reconciled. The condition **R + W > N** guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum intersect in at least one replica, so a read is guaranteed to observe the most recent committed write — this is the quorum analog of the **quorum intersection property** that underlies safety in Paxos as well. Systems like Cassandra expose this as **tunable consistency levels** (`ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, etc.), letting operators trade latency against consistency per-operation rather than system-wide.

Dynamo-style systems also use **sloppy quorums**: rather than requiring responses from the fixed, specific `N` "home" replicas for a key, a write (or read) is accepted from any `W` (or `R`) of the first live nodes encountered while walking the preference list, improving availability under node failure or partition at the cost of weakening the strict intersection guarantee. This pairs with **hinted handoff**: if a replica that should have received a write is down, another node temporarily stores the write along with a "hint" of the intended destination, and forwards it once the destination recovers, restoring full replication without blocking the write. Divergence between replicas that have accepted different concurrent writes is detected via **vector clocks** attached to each value, distinguishing a genuinely concurrent write conflict (requiring application-level or CRDT-based reconciliation) from a simple staleness (a strict causal successor, safely overwriting the older value). Longer-term convergence between replicas that have drifted (e.g., due to extended partitions) is handled by **anti-entropy** protocols using **Merkle trees**: each replica maintains a Merkle tree over its key ranges, and two replicas can compare root hashes and recursively descend into only the subtrees that differ, efficiently identifying the actual divergent keys without comparing every key pairwise. **Read repair** complements this at read time: when a quorum read observes stale replicas among the responses, the coordinator pushes the latest version to those stale replicas opportunistically.

**Paxos** uses quorums differently: a *majority quorum* (any set of more than `N/2` nodes) is required both to complete the prepare/promise phase and the accept phase, and the **quorum intersection property** — any two majority quorums share at least one node — is exactly what guarantees that a value accepted by one majority cannot be silently overwritten by a conflicting value accepted by a disjoint majority, since any later quorum necessarily overlaps with the earlier one and will observe the previously accepted value during the prepare phase. This generalizes beyond strict majorities: **weighted quorums**, **grid quorums**, and **crumbling walls** are alternative quorum constructions that assign votes or geometric structure to nodes to achieve the same intersection guarantee with different availability/load trade-offs — e.g., grid quorums arrange nodes in a logical grid and require one full row plus one element per remaining row, trading higher read cost for lower write cost (or vice versa) compared to flat majority quorums.

The **FLP impossibility result** establishes that no fully asynchronous consensus protocol can guarantee both safety and termination (liveness) if even one process may fail — which is why practical quorum-based consensus protocols (Paxos, Raft) achieve liveness only probabilistically or under partial synchrony assumptions (e.g., eventual leader election via timeouts), not as a deterministic guarantee; safety (never deciding two different values) is preserved unconditionally via the quorum intersection property, while liveness is sacrificed exactly when FLP says it must be. Quorum sizing (how large `R`, `W`, or a consensus quorum must be) is ultimately a concrete expression of the **CAP theorem** trade-off: during a network partition, a system can either shrink its effective quorum to preserve availability (risking inconsistency, as sloppy quorums do) or refuse to serve requests that can't reach a proper quorum (preserving consistency at the cost of availability, as strict majority Paxos quorums do).

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES recovery** proceeds in three passes over the WAL. The **analysis pass** scans forward from the last checkpoint to reconstruct the **transaction table** (which transactions were active at crash time) and the **dirty page table** (which pages had uncommitted changes not yet flushed, and the earliest LSN that might need to be redone for each). The **redo pass** then replays log records starting from the minimum `RecLSN` found in the dirty page table, **repeating history** by reapplying every logged update regardless of whether the modifying transaction eventually committed — redo is made **idempotent** by comparing the log record's LSN against the page's current `PageLSN`, skipping replay if the page already reflects that change, which is what makes it safe to redo even changes whose page already made it to disk before the crash. The **undo pass** then rolls back the (reversed) chronological updates of transactions still active (uncommitted) at crash time, using the log to find each such transaction's chain of updates and writing **CLRs** as it undoes them, so that if a second crash interrupts recovery itself, redo of the CLRs already written ensures the partial undo isn't redone incorrectly — this is the property that makes ARIES-style undo correct even under repeated crashes during recovery.

**Shadow paging** (copy-on-write page-based recovery) is a distinct, logging-free alternative: rather than overwriting modified pages in place, a transaction's writes go to newly allocated shadow copies of the modified pages, while a root/page-table structure continues pointing at the old, unmodified pages; commit is achieved via a single atomic pointer swap of the root table to point at the new pages, after which the old pages can be reclaimed. This avoids needing undo (uncommitted work is simply abandoned, never linked into the live tree) and needs no redo (committed changes are already in place), but it fragments data layout, complicates concurrent transactions (since in-place sharing between transactions is harder when every writer copies pages), and makes it harder to support fine-grained concurrency compared to logging-based schemes, which is why most production systems chose WAL+ARIES over shadow paging.

**Torn-page protection** addresses a hardware-level problem: a page write (e.g., 16 KB) can be interrupted mid-write by a crash or power loss, leaving the page physically mixed between old and new content at the disk sector level — undetectable by the logical redo/undo logic above if left unaddressed. InnoDB's **doublewrite buffer** mitigates this by first writing a batch of dirty pages sequentially to a contiguous doublewrite buffer area on disk (a single large sequential write, cheap and far less likely to tear), fsyncing that, and only then writing each page to its real location; if a crash tears a page during the second write, the intact copy in the doublewrite buffer is used to repair it before normal recovery proceeds. **Page checksums** (stored in each page's header/trailer) provide a complementary, cheaper detection mechanism: a page read back with a checksum mismatch is known to be corrupt or torn, triggering recovery via the WAL or doublewrite buffer rather than silently serving corrupted data.

Distributed crash recovery adds the problem of **in-doubt transactions**: a participant in a 2PC protocol that crashes after logging a `PREPARE` vote but before receiving the coordinator's decision must, upon restart, replay its WAL to discover the in-doubt transaction, then query the coordinator (or a recovery/transaction-status service) to learn the actual outcome before it can release locks and complete redo/undo — a transaction-manager-level recovery process layered on top of the local ARIES-style recovery each participant also performs for its own node crash.

---

Answer: The brief above (sections 1–8) provides the requested exhaustive coverage: WAL via ARIES/LSNs/CLRs/group-commit/checkpointing/physiological logging and Postgres/InnoDB/SQLite implementation differences; MVCC via Postgres xmin/xmax snapshot isolation, undo-log MVCC (Oracle/InnoDB), SSI with rw-antidependency "dangerous structure" detection, Thomas write rule/MVTO, and OCC; LSM trees via memtables/WAL, size-tiered vs leveled (RocksDB L0-Ln) vs universal compaction, bloom filters, and tombstone lifecycle; B+tree maintenance via node split/merge, latch crabbing, blink-tree right-sibling pointers, and foster trees; two-phase commit via prepare/commit phases, the blocking/in-doubt problem, 3PC's CanCommit/PreCommit/DoCommit, presumed-abort/presumed-commit, XA/JTA, and Spanner's 2PC-over-Paxos composition; logical clocks via Lamport clocks, vector clocks, version vectors, HLC, and TrueTime/commit-wait; quorum systems via Dynamo N/R/W with sloppy quorums/hinted handoff/Merkle-tree anti-entropy, Paxos majority-quorum intersection, and grid/weighted quorum constructions tied to FLP and CAP; and crash recovery via ARIES's three-pass analysis/redo/undo with idempotent LSN-based redo and CLR-safe undo, shadow paging as a logging-free alternative, and doublewrite-buffer/checksum torn-page protection plus distributed in-doubt transaction recovery.

# Single-Node Database Storage Internals: WAL, Crash Recovery, and B+Tree Maintenance

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging

The foundational invariant of WAL is simple to state and consequential in implementation: no data page may be written to stable storage until the log records describing the changes to that page have themselves reached stable storage. This gives the system the ability to reconstruct any lost in-memory state from the log, which is the entire basis for crash recovery without requiring every transaction to force its dirty pages to disk at commit.

**ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics)**, developed by Mohan et al. at IBM, is the reference protocol most real engines approximate. ARIES assigns every log record a monotonically increasing **log sequence number (LSN)**. Each data page stores the LSN of the last log record that modified it (the PageLSN), and each log record stores the LSN of the previous log record written by the same transaction (PrevLSN), forming a backward-chained per-transaction log. ARIES is built on three principles: write-ahead logging itself, repeating history during redo (every update, committed or not, is reapplied during redo to bring the database to the exact state at crash time), and logging changes during undo via **compensation log records (CLRs)** so that undo actions themselves are never re-undone. ARIES uses **physiological logging**: a log record identifies the page and operation but the operation may be expressed at a level that is physical in the sense of being tied to a specific page, yet logically composed in that a single logical operation (e.g., delete a key from a B+tree leaf) may log a single record even though its physical byte-level effect depends on the page's current layout. This sits between pure **physical logging** (recording exact byte-level before/after images of a page region) and pure **logical logging** (recording only the logical operation, e.g., "delete key K from index I," with no reference to physical page layout). Physiological logging is chosen because pure physical logging bloats log volume and pure logical logging complicates idempotent redo and undo during recovery when the physical page structure is uncertain.

**Log force-at-commit** is the durability rule: before a transaction's commit can be acknowledged to the client, all log records for that transaction up to and including the commit record must be durably flushed, typically via `fsync()` or `fdatasync()` on the log file, or via direct I/O (`O_DIRECT`) writes that bypass the OS page cache to avoid double-buffering and to get synchronous completion guarantees from the storage device. This is the WAL durability contract underlying the "D" in ACID. Because fsync latency dominates commit latency under high concurrency, **group commit** (also called commit batching or log batching) amortizes this cost: the log manager delays the flush briefly to collect commit records from multiple concurrently committing transactions into a single sequential write, then performs one fsync and releases all waiting transactions together. This trades a small amount of added latency per transaction for a large increase in commit throughput, since sequential log writes are cheap relative to fsync/flush overhead and device command queuing. PostgreSQL implements this via `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings` and via its WAL writer process; InnoDB implements it through the log buffer and `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit` settings controlling exactly how aggressively group commit batches are flushed versus committed asynchronously.

**Checkpointing** bounds recovery time by establishing a point before which all necessary redo work is known to be reflected on disk, so recovery need not scan the log back to the beginning of time. A **consistent checkpoint** (sometimes called a sharp checkpoint) quiesces all active transactions, flushes all dirty buffer pool pages to disk, and writes a checkpoint record, but this stalls the system and is unacceptable for online workloads. A **fuzzy checkpoint**, used by ARIES and virtually all production engines, does not stop transaction processing: it records the current contents of the **transaction table** and **dirty page table (DPT)** (including each dirty page's RecLSN, the LSN at which it first became dirty) into the log, without forcing those dirty pages to disk at that instant. The system continues writing new log records and flushing dirty pages via the ordinary buffer manager in the background; recovery uses the minimum RecLSN across the DPT snapshot to determine where the redo pass must begin. PostgreSQL's checkpointer process performs fuzzy checkpoints, writing a checkpoint record into WAL that records the redo starting LSN; InnoDB performs continuous fuzzy checkpointing tracked via the **checkpoint LSN** and the **redo log's circular buffer**, ensuring the oldest dirty page's LSN in the buffer pool never falls so far behind the log head that the circular redo log would need to wrap over unflushed data (this is the "furious flushing" scenario InnoDB tries to avoid via adaptive flushing).

Different systems diverge meaningfully in WAL granularity and scope. **PostgreSQL's WAL** is a single, server-wide, strictly physical-ish redo log recording changes at the page level for heap and index pages (with specialized "generic WAL" and resource-manager-specific record formats per access method), used purely for crash recovery and replication (streaming/physical replication ships WAL records directly); PostgreSQL has no separate undo log because it uses multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) with tuple versioning and relies on VACUUM rather than log-based undo to reclaim space from aborted/old versions. **SQLite's WAL mode** (an alternative to its default rollback-journal mode) is a single append-only file per database connection set that stores full new page images keyed by page number and a WAL-index (shared memory `-wal` file plus `-shm` hash index) to allow readers to find the latest committed version of each page without blocking writers; periodic **checkpointing** copies WAL frames back into the main database file and truncates/reuses the WAL. This is fundamentally different from ARIES-style redo/undo logging because SQLite's WAL stores whole-page after-images rather than diffs, trading log volume for recovery and concurrency simplicity. **InnoDB's redo log** is physiological, circular, fixed-capacity (sized by `innodb_redo_log_capacity`/historically `innodb_log_file_size`), and strictly redo-only like PostgreSQL's — but InnoDB additionally maintains the **undo log** as a separate structure stored in undo tablespaces/undo segments (part of the rollback segment mechanism inherited from Oracle-style MVCC), used both for transaction rollback and for MVCC consistent-read snapshots, with undo log records themselves being protected by the write-ahead redo log (modifications to undo pages are redo-logged too).

Finally, the log buffer itself typically uses **log-structured buffering**: an in-memory ring buffer accumulates log records sequentially as transactions generate them; a background log writer thread flushes contiguous ranges to the log file(s) either on checkpoint, on buffer-full, or on commit-driven group-commit triggers. Sequential append-only writes to the log device are what make WAL cheap relative to random-write data page flushes, and is why log devices benefit disproportionately from low-latency sequential-write-optimized storage (NVMe, battery-backed write cache, or in cloud contexts, provisioned IOPS volumes dedicated to the log).

## 2. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery** is the canonical algorithm and proceeds in strictly ordered phases, each with a distinct purpose, run once on restart after a crash.

The **analysis pass** scans forward from the most recent checkpoint's recorded redo LSN to the end of the log (the point of crash), reconstructing two in-memory structures that were lost when the system went down: the **transaction table** (listing transactions active at crash time, each with its last LSN and state) and the **dirty page table** (listing pages that were modified in the buffer pool but possibly not yet flushed, each with a RecLSN marking the earliest log record that could have dirtied it). Analysis determines the starting point for the redo pass as the minimum RecLSN across the dirty page table, since any page with RecLSN less than that point is guaranteed already durable.

The **redo pass** replays history starting from that minimum RecLSN forward to the end of the log, reapplying every logged update — regardless of whether its transaction ultimately committed or aborted — to the affected pages. This is the "repeat history" principle: rather than trying to distinguish committed from uncommitted work during redo, ARIES redoes everything and defers the distinction to the undo pass, which considerably simplifies the redo logic. Redo is made **idempotent** via LSN comparison: for each log record being replayed, the recovery process compares the log record's LSN against the target page's current PageLSN (stored in the page header); if PageLSN ≥ the log record's LSN, the update is already reflected on the page (it was flushed before the crash) and the redo action is skipped. This comparison is what allows redo to be safely re-run even if a second crash occurs mid-recovery — the process is naturally idempotent because already-applied updates are detected and skipped rather than reapplied.

The **undo pass** rolls back all transactions that were active (neither committed nor fully rolled back) at crash time, in reverse LSN order, following each transaction's PrevLSN chain backward. Each undo action is itself logged as a **compensation log record (CLR)**: a CLR records the physical inverse of the action being undone and additionally stores a field (ARIES calls this the UndoNxtLSN) pointing to the LSN that should be undone next for that transaction, explicitly skipping over the log record just undone. CLRs are never themselves undone — this is the mechanism that guarantees undo is idempotent and that recovery terminates correctly even if the undo pass is itself interrupted by a second crash: on the next recovery attempt, analysis will see the CLRs already written, and undo will simply continue following UndoNxtLSN pointers without redoing work already compensated.

**Shadow paging** (also called copy-on-write page mapping) is a historically significant alternative to logging-based recovery, used in some early systems (e.g., early versions of System R research prototypes) and conceptually underlying modern copy-on-write filesystems/engines. Rather than modifying pages in place and logging the change, a transaction writes modified pages to new physical locations, leaving the original page untouched, and maintains a shadow page table mapping logical page numbers to physical locations. Commit is achieved atomically by switching a single root pointer to the new page table version; abort simply discards the new pages and the old root remains valid. This trades the complexity of WAL/ARIES-style logging for the overhead of page-table indirection, fragmentation from abandoning old page versions, and difficulty supporting fine-grained concurrency (since shadow paging tends to force whole-page or whole-tree copy-on-write rather than record-level updates), which is why most OLTP engines abandoned it in favor of logical/physiological WAL. Modern analogues appear in LSM-tree-based and copy-on-write B-tree storage engines (e.g., some embedded KV stores using copy-on-write B-trees like LMDB), which get crash consistency from COW page allocation plus a single atomic meta-page pointer swap rather than a separate redo/undo log.

**Torn-page detection and the InnoDB doublewrite buffer** address a hardware-level problem orthogonal to the logical redo/undo machinery: database pages (commonly 8KB or 16KB) are frequently larger than the atomic write unit guaranteed by the underlying storage device or filesystem (traditionally 512-byte or 4K sectors), so a crash mid-write can leave a page **torn** — part old data, part new data, internally inconsistent and not matching either a valid before- or after-image. Because WAL redo uses physiological operations expecting a sane starting page, a torn page would corrupt redo entirely. InnoDB's **doublewrite buffer** solves this by, before writing dirty pages to their actual tablespace locations, first writing them sequentially to a contiguous reserved area (the doublewrite buffer, historically in the system tablespace, now optionally in separate files) and fsync'ing that write; only after this doublewrite write succeeds does InnoDB proceed to write the pages to their real locations. On recovery, if a page read from its real location fails its checksum (indicating a torn or corrupted write), InnoDB restores the known-good copy from the doublewrite buffer before applying redo. **Page checksums** (InnoDB uses CRC32-based checksums embedded in the page header/trailer; PostgreSQL optionally enables page-level checksums via `initdb --data-checksums`) are the detection mechanism paired with doublewrite/torn-page recovery — read-time checksum verification flags corruption so the system knows to fall back to the doublewrite copy or, in PostgreSQL's case, to report corruption since PostgreSQL does not maintain an equivalent doublewrite buffer and instead relies on `full_page_writes` (logging entire page images to WAL the first time a page is modified after a checkpoint) to achieve the same torn-page protection: on recovery, if full-page-write images exist for a page in the WAL since the last checkpoint, redo restores from the full image rather than trying to apply a physiological delta to a possibly-torn page.

Recovery of **in-doubt distributed transactions** arises when a node participates in a two-phase commit (2PC) protocol as a resource manager and crashes between receiving a PREPARE vote request and receiving the final COMMIT/ABORT decision from the transaction coordinator. The node's local WAL will contain a logged "prepared" record (in ARIES terms, a transaction that reached a prepared state is logged so its locks/resources are held and not unilaterally rolled back) but no commit or abort record. During local crash recovery's analysis pass, such a transaction appears in the transaction table as prepared-but-undetermined; standard ARIES undo must not unilaterally abort it, since the global coordinator may have already decided to commit. The node holds the transaction in this in-doubt state (locks retained, resources pinned) and must query the transaction coordinator (or a transaction manager / XA resource manager log) upon recovery to resolve the outcome, then apply the appropriate redo-commit finalization or undo-abort using the ordinary logged undo/CLR machinery once the decision is known. This is the standard XA/2PC recovery protocol layered on top of local ARIES recovery.

## 3. B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splitting and merging** are the baseline structural modification operations (SMOs) that keep a B+tree balanced under insert/delete. On insert into a full leaf, the leaf splits into two: keys are partitioned (commonly at the midpoint), a new separator key is inserted into the parent pointing at the new right sibling, and if the parent is itself full this propagates upward, potentially splitting the root and increasing tree height by one. On delete, if a node's occupancy falls below a minimum threshold (commonly half of the fill factor), the node either merges with a sibling (if the combined occupancy fits within one page) or borrows/redistributes keys from a sibling to restore minimum occupancy without a full merge; merging similarly can propagate upward, decreasing tree height. Many production engines (e.g., InnoDB) are lazier about merging than classical textbook algorithms specify — they tolerate underfull leaf pages rather than immediately merging on every delete, since eager merging under high-churn workloads causes oscillating split/merge thrashing; InnoDB specifically delays merges and relies on periodic page reorganization instead.

**Latch crabbing (also called lock coupling)** is the standard concurrency control protocol for tree traversal that avoids holding a lock on the entire tree during a single operation. A traversal acquires a latch (a short-duration, low-level mutex distinct from longer-held transactional locks) on the root, then acquires a latch on the relevant child before releasing the parent's latch — hence "crabbing," alternating hand-over-hand down the tree. For read-only traversal, shared latches suffice and can be released as soon as the child latch is acquired. For insert/delete traversal where a split or merge might propagate upward, the naive approach must hold exclusive latches pessimistically on every ancestor from the root down, since any one of them might need modification; an optimization observes that a node is only "safe" (guaranteed not to require propagation) if it is not full (for inserts) or not at minimum occupancy (for deletes), so the traversal can release ancestor latches as soon as it reaches a safe descendant, since that descendant guarantees no propagation above it will be necessary. This dramatically reduces latch contention relative to pessimistically locking the whole root-to-leaf path on every write.

**Structure modification operations (SMOs)** — splits, merges, and redistributions — are the operations that must be made safe under concurrent access without resorting to a tree-wide lock, which is where crabbing alone is insufficient because a split must atomically update both the splitting node and its parent (and possibly propagate further), and other threads must never observe an inconsistent intermediate state (e.g., a leaf that has split but whose parent doesn't yet have a pointer to the new sibling). The classical solution couples latch crabbing with the "safe node" optimization above for the common case, falling back to holding exclusive latches up the whole path only when an SMO is actually needed, and doing the actual multi-page update (writing the new sibling, updating the separator key in the parent, updating sibling pointers) while holding exclusive latches on exactly the nodes being mutated, released in a well-defined order to avoid deadlock (always top-down or using try-latch with backoff).

**B-link trees (B-link / Blink-trees)**, from Lehman and Yao's 1981 paper "Efficient Locking for Concurrent Operations on B-Trees," solve the SMO-concurrency problem differently and are widely used in production engines (and widely cited as the concurrency scheme underlying systems like early IBM and later many open-source B+tree implementations). The key structural addition is a **right-sibling pointer** at every level of the tree (not just leaves) plus a **high-key** on every node recording the maximum key value reachable through that node. A split is performed as two separate atomic steps rather than one: first, the node being split creates its new right sibling and sets its own right-sibling pointer to point to it (and sets its own high-key), making the split locally visible and consistent even before the parent is updated; second, in a separate step, the separator key is posted into the parent. Between these two steps, the tree is in a transiently "incomplete" state, but it is never inconsistent: a concurrent reader or writer who lands on the original (now-split) node looking for a key that moved to the new sibling will find, via the high-key check, that the key it wants exceeds the node's high-key, and will simply follow the right-sibling pointer to find it — a mechanism called "moving right." This means **no node other than the two directly involved in a split ever needs to be latched during the first step**, since any other in-flight traversal can always self-correct by moving right rather than requiring the split to be instantaneously visible everywhere at once. This is the core advantage of B-link trees: readers never block on an in-progress SMO.

The **right-sibling pointer mechanism also provides a recovery benefit**: if a crash occurs between the two steps of a split (node split locally but parent not yet updated with the new separator key), the tree remains structurally traversable and correct purely by the moving-right mechanism — the "incomplete" state is not actually a corruption, it's a tolerated intermediate state, so crash recovery for B-link trees does not need special-case repair logic for interrupted splits; the second step (posting to the parent) can simply be completed lazily, even by an unrelated later traversal that notices the inconsistency and fixes it ("half-split" repair), rather than requiring recovery-time special handling. This is a significant simplification relative to classical B+trees without sibling pointers, where an interrupted split can leave the tree in a state that is only fixable by replaying the exact logged operation.

**Foster trees** (Graefe et al.) extend the B-link idea further for engines needing even cheaper SMOs: rather than only linking split siblings, a foster-child pointer temporarily attaches an overfull node's "soon to be separated" portion as a foster child before the formal split (separator-key insertion into the parent) is completed, allowing the data-moving step and the structural (parent-pointer) step to be fully decoupled in time, which is useful for minimizing the duration for which any latches are held and for integrating cleanly with the kind of write-optimized, log-structured page management used in engines with large SMOs merged with checkpointing/flushing.

Several additional maintenance mechanisms matter for production efficiency rather than pure correctness. **Prefix and suffix truncation** reduces key storage in internal (and sometimes leaf) nodes: internal node separator keys often only need to be long enough to distinguish the two subtrees they separate, so engines store a truncated "minimal distinguishing prefix" rather than the full key, increasing fanout and reducing tree height (this is sometimes called "prefix compression" in index literature and is used in, e.g., InnoDB's and PostgreSQL's B-tree implementations in various forms, as well as being a defining feature of the "Prefix B-tree" variant). **Fill factor** is a tunable target occupancy (e.g., 70–90%) used at index build/bulk-load time and sometimes maintained incrementally, deliberately leaving free space in each page so subsequent inserts can proceed without immediately triggering a split; higher fill factor improves space efficiency and read locality but increases split frequency and write amplification under insert-heavy workloads, while lower fill factor trades space for reduced SMO frequency. **Right-only append and bulk loading** optimizes the common case of monotonically increasing key insertion (e.g., auto-increment primary keys or time-series ingestion): rather than performing a full root-to-leaf traversal with crabbing for each insert, the engine can retain a cached pointer/latch on the rightmost leaf and append directly, falling back to full traversal and split logic only when that rightmost leaf fills; bulk loading an index from sorted input builds the tree bottom-up by packing leaves to a target fill factor and constructing internal levels directly from the resulting leaf boundaries, which is dramatically cheaper than inserting each key individually through the standard insert path since it avoids per-key latch acquisition, random I/O, and incremental SMO propagation entirely.

response.content:
# Technical Brief: MVCC and LSM Trees

## 1. Multi-Version Concurrency Control

### 1.1 Snapshot Isolation via Timestamp Ordering

Snapshot isolation (SI) gives each transaction a consistent view of the database as of a logical start point, implemented through transaction timestamps rather than locking reads against writes. On transaction begin, the system assigns a `start_timestamp` (in Postgres, derived from the current state of `pg_clog`/`pg_xact` combined with an active-transaction snapshot called `ActiveSnapshot`; in systems like Oracle and MySQL/InnoDB, a System Change Number (SCN) or sequence counter). On commit, a `commit_timestamp` is assigned, often via a centralized counter or, in distributed systems, via Lamport clocks, hybrid logical clocks (HLC), or TrueTime-style bounded-uncertainty intervals (Spanner).

A transaction under SI reads only versions whose commit timestamp precedes its own start timestamp and ignores versions from transactions that committed after it began, regardless of physical commit order. This decouples readers from writers entirely — readers never block writers and vice versa — which is the main practical payoff of MVCC over strict two-phase locking (S2PL). The catch is write-write conflicts: SI still requires that two concurrent transactions not both successfully write the same row. This is enforced by one of two canonical conflict-resolution rules:

- **First-committer-wins (FCW)**: when T1 attempts to commit, the system checks whether any concurrently running transaction has already committed a write to a row T1 also wrote. If so, T1 aborts. Postgres uses this rule: it detects the conflict at commit time by checking whether the tuple's current `xmax` was set by a transaction that committed after T1's snapshot was taken.
- **First-updater-wins (FUW)**: the first transaction to *attempt* the write acquires a write lock (or version-level tuple lock) on the row immediately, and the second concurrent updater blocks until the first resolves (commits or aborts), then retries or aborts depending on whether a true conflict remains. InnoDB's implementation of REPEATABLE READ-based snapshot behavior leans toward FUW semantics for row-level UPDATE conflicts.

### 1.2 xmin/xmax Tuple Versioning and Visibility Rules (Postgres Model)

Postgres implements MVCC as an append-only heap where every tuple carries two system columns: `xmin` (the transaction ID that inserted/created this tuple version) and `xmax` (the transaction ID that deleted or superseded it, or 0/invalid if the tuple is still the latest version). An UPDATE is implemented as an atomic pair: the old tuple gets its `xmax` set to the updating transaction's XID, and a new tuple version is appended with `xmin` set to the same XID; a `ctid` forward-pointer chains old tuple to new tuple for index-chasing during visibility checks (HOT - Heap-Only Tuples - optimizes this chain when no indexed column changed).

Visibility of a given tuple version to a transaction T with snapshot S is determined by `HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC`, applying rules roughly of this form:
- tuple is visible if `xmin`'s transaction is committed and committed before S was taken (or is T itself and the command counter permits it), AND
- `xmax` is either invalid, or belongs to a transaction that is aborted, or is still in-progress/committed-after-S from T's point of view.

Because commit status alone (committed/aborted/in-progress) isn't temporally ordered, Postgres cross-references the snapshot's list of XIDs that were active at snapshot-take time (`xip` array) rather than raw timestamps — this is effectively a logical-clock substitute for true commit timestamps, avoiding a global timestamp bottleneck. Transaction status is tracked in the commit log (`pg_xact`, formerly `pg_clog`), a bitmap of XID → {in-progress, committed, aborted, sub-committed}.

### 1.3 Vacuum, Garbage Collection, and the xmin Horizon

Because Postgres never overwrites or physically deletes tuple versions in place, dead tuple versions (superseded by newer `xmin`/`xmax` chains) accumulate as heap bloat. The `VACUUM` process (and `autovacuum` daemon) reclaims this space by scanning for tuples whose `xmax` transaction has committed and whose version is no longer visible to *any* currently active or future snapshot, then marking the line pointer as reusable (via the free space map, FSM) or, for `VACUUM FULL`, physically compacting the heap.

The critical correctness constraint is the **xmin horizon** (also called the oldest active snapshot's xmin, tracked via `pg_stat_activity.backend_xmin` and the global `RecentGlobalXmin`/`GlobalVisState` in modern Postgres): a dead tuple cannot be reclaimed if any still-running transaction's snapshot could theoretically still need to see it, because that transaction began before the tuple's `xmax` committed. A long-running transaction (or an idle-in-transaction session, or an uncommitted prepared transaction from 2PC, or a stale replication slot holding back `catalog_xmin`) pins the xmin horizon low, preventing vacuum from advancing — this is the mechanism behind "vacuum can't keep up" bloat incidents and, in extreme cases, transaction ID wraparound failure.

InnoDB's equivalent garbage collection is **purge**, which removes old versions from the undo log/rollback segments once no active read view can reference them; it is governed by `trx_sys->rsegs` and the oldest active read view's "view low limit," structurally the same concept as the xmin horizon but implemented over undo-segment chains rather than an append-only heap.

### 1.4 Undo-Log-Based MVCC vs Append-Only Heap MVCC

Two fundamentally different physical strategies implement the same logical MVCC semantics:

**Undo-log-based (Oracle, InnoDB):** The current tuple is stored in place in the primary data page; old versions are *not* kept inline but reconstructed on demand by applying undo records from rollback segments (Oracle) or the undo tablespace (InnoDB) in reverse. A reader needing an old version follows a roll pointer (`DB_ROLL_PTR` in InnoDB) from the current row to its most recent undo record, and potentially further back through a chain, reconstructing the version as of its read view. This keeps the primary table compact (no bloat from old versions sitting in the main heap) but makes long-running transactions expensive, since purge cannot reclaim undo segments while any read view might need them, and reconstructing far-back versions means walking long undo chains ("long rollback segment" pathologies, visible in InnoDB as "trx rollback" slowness).

**Append-only (Postgres heap):** Every version, old and new, lives directly in the heap as a distinct physical tuple; there's no reconstruction step, visibility is a direct predicate check on the tuple's own `xmin`/`xmax`. This makes reads of historical-but-still-visible versions cheap (no chain-walking) at the cost of heap bloat and the need for vacuum as a continuous background cost. It also means index entries can point directly at physical tuple versions (subject to bloat and the need for index-only-scan visibility map tricks).

### 1.5 Timestamp Ordering, Thomas Write Rule, and MVTO

Classical timestamp-ordering (T/O) concurrency control, distinct from lock-based schemes, assigns each transaction a unique timestamp at start and enforces that all reads/writes execute as if transactions ran in timestamp order. Each data item tracks `read_timestamp` (RTS, the largest timestamp of any transaction that read it) and `write_timestamp` (WTS, the largest timestamp of any transaction that wrote it). A write by transaction T with timestamp ts(T) is rejected if ts(T) < RTS(item) (a transaction with smaller timestamp would be writing a value that a "later" transaction already read — violates serializability) or if ts(T) < WTS(item) under the basic rule.

The **Thomas Write Rule** is a specific optimization to basic T/O: if ts(T) < WTS(item) but ts(T) ≥ RTS(item) (no one has read the intervening value), the write can simply be *ignored* rather than aborting the transaction — the write is logically overwritten by a more recent write anyway, so skipping it preserves an equivalent serializable order. This relaxes basic T/O into a non-serializability-violating form that improves throughput by converting what would be unnecessary aborts into silent no-ops.

**Multi-Version Timestamp Ordering (MVTO)** extends T/O by retaining multiple versions per item instead of overwriting in place: each write creates a new version tagged with the writer's timestamp; a read by transaction T is routed to the version with the largest write-timestamp ≤ ts(T), and that version's read-timestamp is bumped to max(RTS, ts(T)) to record the read for future write-ordering checks. Because multiple versions exist, reads never block or abort — this is the theoretical ancestor of systems like Postgres's and InnoDB's practical MVCC, though MVTO as classically defined uses true timestamps for ordering (rather than Postgres's XID+snapshot substitute) and can guarantee serializability, not merely snapshot isolation, when combined with proper write-timestamp conflict checks.

### 1.6 Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) Validation Phases

OCC (Kung & Robinson) structures each transaction into three phases:
1. **Read phase**: the transaction reads from a private/local workspace, buffering all writes locally without touching shared state or acquiring locks.
2. **Validation phase**: at commit time, the system checks whether the transaction's read set and write set conflict with any concurrently validated/committed transaction. Backward validation checks against already-committed transactions; forward validation checks against still-active ones. The check is essentially: for each transaction Tj that committed (or is validating) with a timestamp between T's start and T's validation time, verify that WriteSet(Tj) ∩ ReadSet(T) = ∅ (no write-read conflict with an intervening transaction).
3. **Write phase**: if validation succeeds, buffered writes are applied/installed atomically; otherwise the transaction aborts and retries.

OCC performs best under low contention, since it never blocks during the read phase but pays for conflicts entirely at commit time via abort-and-retry — the inverse risk profile of pessimistic locking. Modern main-memory OLTP systems (e.g., Hekaton's OCC implementation in SQL Server, Silo) combine OCC validation with MVCC-style multi-versioning: readers get a consistent snapshot via version chains, and the validation phase checks a transaction's read set against version visibility rather than raw item locks, often using a single global epoch/TID counter to batch validation cheaply (as in Silo's "tid" scheme, which also piggybacks the Thomas-Write-Rule-like idea of skipping redundant overwrite checks).

### 1.7 Write Skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

Snapshot isolation prevents the "lost update" anomaly via first-committer/first-updater-wins conflict detection, but it does **not** prevent **write skew**: a scenario where two transactions each read an overlapping data set, each independently satisfy a constraint based on what they read, and then each write to *disjoint* items such that the combined effect of both commits violates the constraint, even though neither transaction's write set overlaps the other's write set (classic example: two on-call doctors each check that at least one other doctor is on call before taking themselves off call — both snapshots show two on-call doctors, both go off call, ending with zero). Because FCW/FUW only looks at write-write conflicts on the same row, this passes undetected under plain SI.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, due to Cahill, Röhm, and Fekete and implemented in Postgres as `SERIALIZABLE` isolation level, detects and aborts transactions that would produce non-serializable write-skew anomalies on top of an SI substrate. SSI tracks **rw-antidependencies** — edges in a transaction dependency graph representing "T1 read a version that T2 later overwrote" (as opposed to ww-dependencies already handled by SI's conflict rule, or wr-dependencies which are regular dependencies). The key theoretical result (Fekete et al.) is that any non-serializable execution under SI must contain a **"dangerous structure"**: two consecutive rw-antidependency edges forming a cycle pattern T1 → T2 → T3 where T1 and T3 may be the same transaction, with both edges being rw-antidependencies and at least one of the transactions being concurrent (not already serialized) with its neighbors. SSI's runtime detects this pattern incrementally: Postgres tracks, per tuple, which transactions read it (`SIREAD` locks, which are not real locks but conflict-tracking markers) and flags an antidependency whenever a write is detected against a tuple someone concurrently holds an SIREAD marker for. When the dangerous-structure pattern (two rw-edges in sequence, with the pivot transaction concurrent with both neighbors) is detected, one of the transactions (typically the one that would complete the cycle) is aborted, guaranteeing serializable outcomes without ever constructing the full precedence graph or taking read locks that would block concurrent access.

---

## 2. Log-Structured Merge Trees

### 2.1 Memtable, WAL, and the Flush Pipeline

An LSM tree absorbs all writes into an in-memory sorted structure called the **memtable**, typically backed by a **skiplist** (used in LevelDB, RocksDB's default memtable implementation, and Cassandra) because skiplists give O(log n) expected insert/lookup/range-scan with simpler lock-free or fine-grained-locking concurrent implementations than balanced binary trees; some engines (RocksDB has pluggable memtable factories) alternatively use a hash-linked-list or a vector memtable optimized for bulk-load/sequential-insert workloads.

Before being applied to the memtable, every write is first appended to a **write-ahead log (WAL)** on durable storage, satisfying the standard durability requirement: a crash after fsync-ing the WAL record but before the memtable write (or before flush) can still be recovered by replaying the WAL from the last durable point. The WAL is purely sequential-append, making it cheap relative to the random-access cost that would be incurred writing directly to a sorted on-disk structure.

Once the memtable reaches a size threshold, it is frozen (made immutable) and a background thread flushes it to disk as a new **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** — an immutable, sorted, on-disk file. A fresh empty memtable (plus a fresh WAL segment) is swapped in to absorb further writes, so writers are never blocked except transiently during the swap. This flush is itself a sequential write of already-sorted data, which is the central efficiency property of LSM trees: both the WAL append and the SSTable flush are sequential I/O, avoiding the random-write penalty that a B-tree incurs on every leaf-page update.

### 2.2 SSTable Format, Block Indexes, and Sparse Indexes

An SSTable is organized as a sequence of fixed-size **data blocks**, each holding a sorted run of key-value entries (often delta/prefix-compressed since adjacent keys within a sorted block share prefixes), followed by an **index block** mapping each data block's last (or first) key to that block's file offset — this is a **sparse index**: rather than indexing every key, it indexes only block boundaries, trading a small amount of extra scanning-within-a-block for a dramatically smaller in-memory index footprint. A point lookup for key K binary-searches the sparse index to find the candidate block, then linearly (or via block-local binary search, for formats with intra-block restart points like LevelDB's/RocksDB's block format) scans within that block.

Each SSTable additionally carries a **footer/metadata block** with pointers to the index block, a **bloom filter** block (see below), and often per-SSTable metadata like the smallest/largest key, sequence number range, and table properties used by compaction heuristics. RocksDB's specific `BlockBasedTable` format layers this further with a **partitioned index** for very large SSTables (splitting the index itself into blocks, since a single index block for a huge file would itself become too large to cache) and an optional **top-level index** over those index partitions.

### 2.3 Bloom Filters for Point-Lookup Avoidance

Because a point lookup in an LSM tree may need to probe multiple SSTables across multiple levels (the key could reside in any of them, since newer writes shadow older ones but the engine doesn't know a priori which file holds it), LSM engines attach a **Bloom filter** to each SSTable (or each block, for RocksDB's "full filter" vs older "block-based filter" modes) summarizing its key set. A Bloom filter is a probabilistic set-membership structure: an array of `m` bits and `k` hash functions; insertion sets `k` bits per key, and a query checks whether all `k` corresponding bits are set. It never produces false negatives (if the filter says "not present," the key is definitely absent, so the SSTable can be skipped entirely) but has a tunable **false positive rate**, meaning the filter may say "maybe present" for a key not actually in the table, forcing an unnecessary disk read.

The false positive rate is governed by `m/n` (bits per key) and `k`; the optimal `k` for a given bits-per-key ratio is `k ≈ (m/n) · ln(2)`, and RocksDB's default configuration uses roughly 10 bits per key yielding ~1% false positive rate, tunable via `BlockBasedTableOptions::filter_policy` (`NewBloomFilterPolicy(bits_per_key)`). Increasing bits-per-key reduces false positives (hence fewer wasted disk reads) at the cost of more memory/disk space for the filter itself — a direct space/read-amplification trade-off. RocksDB also supports **Ribbon filters**, a newer, more space-efficient alternative to classic Bloom filters offering a better space/false-positive-rate trade-off via a different encoding (based on structured Gaussian elimination over a randomized linear system), without changing the underlying "skip the SSTable entirely on negative" usage pattern.

### 2.4 Compaction Strategies: Size-Tiered vs Leveled vs Hybrid

Because every flush produces a new SSTable, and because multiple SSTables may each hold different versions (or tombstones) of the same key, the LSM tree periodically **compacts** — merges multiple SSTables into fewer, larger ones, applying standard k-way merge-sort logic exploiting the fact that each input SSTable is already internally sorted, discarding obsolete/overwritten versions and resolving tombstones along the way. Compaction strategy is the dominant lever controlling the read-amplification/write-amplification/space-amplification trade-off triangle:

- **Size-tiered compaction strategy (STCS)** (used by default in Cassandra, and as RocksDB's "universal compaction"): SSTables are grouped into tiers by similar size; when enough similarly-sized SSTables accumulate at a tier (e.g., 4 tables of similar size), they are merged into one larger SSTable promoted to the next tier. This minimizes write amplification (data is rewritten relatively few times across its lifetime) but at the cost of higher space amplification (multiple full generations of data may coexist temporarily, and duplicate/overwritten versions linger longer before being merged away) and higher read amplification for point lookups (a key may need to be checked in many tiers before being found, though Bloom filters mitigate the I/O cost).

- **Leveled compaction strategy (LCS)**, as implemented in LevelDB and as RocksDB's default (`kCompactionStyleLevel`): data is organized into levels L0, L1, ..., Ln with exponentially increasing size targets (commonly a 10x size multiplier between levels). L0 holds raw flushed memtables (files that may have overlapping key ranges with each other, since they come straight from sequential memtable flushes); L1 and beyond are maintained with **non-overlapping key ranges** within a level, allowing a point lookup at L1+ to binary-search to exactly one candidate file per level rather than checking all files. Compaction from Li to Li+1 picks one (or a few) SSTable(s) from Li and merges them against all overlapping SSTables in Li+1, producing new non-overlapping SSTables for Li+1. This bounds space amplification tightly (roughly 1.1x of the logical data size, since old versions are eagerly purged on every compaction pass) and bounds read amplification (at most one file check per level, excluding L0), at the cost of significantly higher write amplification — each key may be rewritten once per level it passes through as data cascades downward (commonly cited worst-case ~10x-30x write amplification for deep level counts under a 10x per-level size ratio).

- **Tiered+leveled hybrids**: RocksDB's "universal compaction" (a size-tiered-style scheme) and tiered-leveled hybrids used by systems like ScyllaDB or TiDB's Titan engine combine the approaches — e.g., treating L0 with size-tiered-style merging to minimize write amplification for hot recent data while maintaining strict leveled non-overlap further down the tree to bound space/read amplification for cold data. This is a deliberate point on the same three-way trade-off triangle (read amp / write amp / space amp), rather than a free lunch — tuning parameters like `level0_file_num_compaction_trigger`, `max_bytes_for_level_base`, and `target_file_size_base` in RocksDB let operators shift along that trade-off curve.

### 2.5 Tombstones, Deletion, and Compaction-Time Removal

Because SSTables are immutable, a delete cannot physically remove a key from an already-flushed file; instead, a delete is recorded as a **tombstone** — a special marker record (in RocksDB, a `kTypeDeletion` entry; Cassandra additionally supports range tombstones covering a key range) written through the same memtable → WAL → SSTable flush path as a normal write, carrying the same sequence number ordering semantics so that a tombstone correctly shadows older versions of the key at lower levels/older SSTables while itself being visible to reads as "this key does not exist."

A tombstone is only safely and permanently removable during compaction, and only once the compaction has merged across *all* levels/SSTables that could possibly contain an older version of that key — removing a tombstone prematurely (while an older version of the key still exists in a lower level not participating in the current compaction) would cause the deleted key to "resurrect." RocksDB and LevelDB handle this by only dropping tombstones when compacting down to the bottom-most level (or more precisely, when the compaction's input/output level range is known to subsume every possible location of an older version — tracked via metadata like `bottommost_level` flags and bloom-filter/seqnum range checks). Range tombstones in particular (used for RocksDB's `DeleteRange` and Cassandra's partition/range deletes) require special compaction-time handling since they can shadow arbitrarily many keys without an explicit per-key marker, and are tracked via a separate tombstone fragment index merged against data blocks during both reads and compaction.

Until removed, tombstones contribute directly to both read amplification (reads must scan past them, and range scans in particular can be slowed drastically by long tombstone runs — the classic Cassandra "tombstone storm" pathology) and space amplification, which is why compaction scheduling heuristics in RocksDB (e.g., `periodic_compaction_seconds`, and TTL-aware compaction) often deliberately force otherwise-unnecessary compactions purely to expire old tombstones and reclaim space.

### 2.6 Write and Read Amplification Trade-offs

**Write amplification** is the ratio of physical bytes written to storage versus logical bytes written by the application; in LSM trees it arises because a single logical write is first written to the WAL, then to the memtable (in-memory, not counted physically), then flushed to an SSTable at L0, then rewritten at every subsequent compaction pass as it cascades through L1...Ln. Leveled compaction incurs the highest write amplification of common strategies precisely because of this cascading rewrite; this is the direct price paid for leveled compaction's tight space-amplification and read-amplification bounds.

**Read amplification** is the number of physical I/O operations (disk reads) needed to satisfy one logical read, driven by how many distinct SSTables (and within each, how many blocks) might need to be checked: for a point lookup, this is roughly (files in L0 that might overlap) + (one file per subsequent level, under leveled compaction's non-overlap invariant) + (block index/data block reads per candidate file) — mitigated heavily by Bloom filters eliminating most non-matching SSTables without an actual disk read, and by block caches (RocksDB's `BlockCache`, an in-memory LRU of recently-read data/index/filter blocks) absorbing hot-path reads entirely in memory. Range scans amplify differently: they must merge-iterate across all overlapping SSTables regardless of Bloom filters (which only help point lookups), so range-scan read amplification is driven primarily by the number of overlapping files touched, which is why size-tiered strategies (with more overlapping files per tier) tend to have worse range-scan behavior than leveled strategies.

These two amplification metrics plus **space amplification** (ratio of physical bytes on disk to logical live data size, driven by un-compacted duplicate/overwritten versions and un-expired tombstones) form the standard three-way trade-off; no compaction strategy minimizes all three simultaneously, and system tuning (choice of STCS vs LCS vs universal/hybrid, per-level size multipliers, compaction trigger thresholds, Bloom filter bits-per-key) is fundamentally about choosing a deliberate operating point on that trade-off surface for the target workload (write-heavy vs point-lookup-heavy vs range-scan-heavy).
